title: The Fourteenth Dalai Lama
hookLine: a monk and teacher in exile since 1959, known for kindness as his religion

cards: Ask him what he is, and the answer usually comes back simple: a Buddhist monk. Not a king, not a god-king, not a celebrity, though his face hangs in homes and on posters.
A monk who gets up early, sits, studies and recites, the way monks in his tradition do. He laughs a lot in interviews, and he keeps bringing the conversation back to one thing.
When people ask about his religion, he has said it is very simple: kindness.

teach.b: In Tibetan Buddhism, his followers understand the Dalai Lama as a teacher who returns, life after life, as an emanation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.

Tradition says that when one Dalai Lama dies, senior lamas search for the child in whom he has returned, using signs, visions and tests. The present Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, is the fourteenth in that line.

teach.h: FOUND AS A CHILD, TRAINED IN LHASA.
teach.b: He was found as a small boy in a farming village and brought to Lhasa to be trained.

During the Chinese takeover of Tibet, he fled across the mountains into India. He has lived there ever since, with a community of Tibetans around him in Dharamsala, teaching, writing and meeting people from everywhere.
Not everyone sees him the same way. For Tibetans who follow him he is a spiritual guide and a symbol of home. The government of China disputes his role.

Some Tibetan Buddhists follow other lamas first. Here, though, the interest is what he teaches. He studied the long, hard texts of Tibetan philosophy and earned the geshe degree, a title for monk-scholars.

teach.h: KINDNESS AS TRAINING, NOT A MOOD.
teach.b: Yet with wide audiences he keeps returning to compassion and kindness, which he calls the root of the practice, and he says these don't belong to Buddhists alone. Kindness, as he describes it, isn't softness.
It's training: noticing that other people want happiness and don't want to suffer, just as you do, and letting that change how you act. Practiced again and again, until it becomes habit.
That's what turns kindness from a mood into a practice.

how: Tibetan Buddhists attend the Dalai Lama's public teachings in Dharamsala and elsewhere, and practice compassion trainings in which they reflect that all beings want happiness and do not want suffering.

games.q: the Fourteenth Dalai Lama: tap the pairs.

s: he describes himself as a god-king
he usually calls himself a simple Buddhist monk.
tradition says lamas search for the child in whom the Dalai Lama returns
he teaches that compassion belongs to Buddhists alone

games.q: someone asks the Dalai Lama to sum up his religion in a word. what does he say?
games.why: he has said his religion is very simple: kindness. the long philosophy is there too, but he keeps coming back to this.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today, not your favorite person, just someone, and say quietly: this person wants to be happy, just like me; this person doesn't want to suffer, just like me.
Then try the same two lines with someone who annoys you. Don't force a warm feeling; just notice what the words do.

wordCard.voice: Tenzin Gyatso, the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, a Tibetan monk and teacher living in exile, who calls kindness the heart of his practice.

orig.note: Sanskrit Avalokiteshvara: the bodhisattva of compassion, whom the Dalai Lamas are held to emanate.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness as practice. They want happiness too, just like you. Go gently.
